question:
Patient note:
A 62-year-old woman presented to the general medicine consult service at the request of her oncologist because of progressive aching in the right calf with exertion and a new non-healing fissure at the tip of the third toe, both of which have evolved over the prior six weeks while she has been receiving palliative systemic therapy for hormone-receptor–positive breast carcinoma first discovered five years earlier. The malignancy was originally treated with lumpectomy, axillary node dissection, adjuvant radiation, and an aromatase inhibitor; however, two years ago she developed low-back pain and work-up revealed multiple sclerotic lesions in the thoracic and lumbar spine consistent with osseous spread. More recently, staging positron-emission tomography performed three months ago demonstrated additional uptake in the right iliac crest as well as small bilateral pulmonary nodules that were deemed consistent with further metastatic involvement. She is currently midway through her sixth cycle of capecitabine and ribociclib, has not yet required bisphosphonate infusions, and has never undergone hepatic resection, stereotactic brain radiation, or enrollment in investigational protocols. She has no history of lymphoma or other hematologic malignancy. 

Her past medical history is also notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed at age 56 during evaluation for polyuria; the condition has been managed with lifestyle modification plus metformin 1000 mg twice daily, and her most recent hemoglobin A1c checked six weeks earlier was 6.9 %. She reports no episodes of hyperglycemic crisis, visual changes, paresthesias, or proteinuria, and annual ophthalmologic screening last autumn revealed only mild background retinal changes without edema. She denies any prior episodes of crushing substernal chest tightness, emergent catheterization, coronary stent placement, or heart muscle weakness; she sleeps on a single pillow, climbs one flight of stairs without orthopnea, and has never been told she had fluid around the lungs. She has never been informed that she suffered a heart attack, and no clinician has diagnosed her with heart failure. She also denies transient speech difficulty, facial asymmetry, unilateral limb weakness, or episodes suggestive of cerebral infarction. 

Regarding the lower-extremity discomfort, she can ambulate approximately one city block before a cramping sensation develops behind the right knee and radiates into the calf; the discomfort resolves within two minutes of rest and predictably recurs with renewed effort. Nine months earlier she underwent duplex ultrasonography that showed mild atherosclerotic plaque but no flow-limiting stenosis, and she was advised to begin daily aspirin and high-intensity statin therapy. She has never undergone bypass grafting or endovascular stenting of the limb vessels and denies digital discoloration or rest pain until the recent toe lesion appeared. She stopped smoking 25 pack-years ago at the time of her cancer diagnosis and drinks wine only on holidays; she has never used illicit drugs. There is no family history of premature coronary disease, early stroke, connective-tissue disorders, or peptic ulcer disease. Current medications include metformin, aspirin 81 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, letrozole, ribociclib, capecitabine, and vitamin D; she takes no corticosteroids or anticoagulants. 

Review of systems is negative for chronic cough, wheezing, abdominal pain, hematemesis, melena, jaundice, photosensitivity rash, oral ulcers, fevers, or night sweats. She has never had a diagnosed gastric or duodenal ulcer or required therapy for peptic ulcer disease. There is no personal history of rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, scleroderma, or other connective-tissue diseases. 

In clinic she appeared well nourished but fatigued; vital signs showed temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 132/78 mm Hg in the right arm while seated, heart rate 82 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98 % on room air. Body mass index was 29 kg/m². Cardiovascular examination revealed normal S1 and S2 without gallops or murmurs and no jugular venous distention. Lungs were clear to auscultation with good air entry bilaterally. The abdomen was soft, non-tender, with a liver edge that was smooth and palpable 1 cm below the costal margin; there was no splenomegaly, shifting dullness, or abdominal wall collateral veins, and she has never been diagnosed with chronic hepatitis or cirrhosis. On vascular inspection of the lower limbs, dorsalis pedis pulse on the right was 1+ compared with 2+ on the left; posterior tibial pulses were similarly asymmetric, and capillary refill in the right toes was mildly delayed. A 0.8-cm superficial ulcer with a pale base and minimal serous drainage was noted at the distal third toe without surrounding cellulitis. There was no lower-extremity edema or varicosities. 

Neurologic exam demonstrated intact cranial nerves, full strength, normal sensation to light touch and monofilament testing throughout the feet, symmetrical reflexes, and coordinated gait limited only by calf pain. Cognition is intact; she is fully oriented, recalls three objects at five minutes, follows complex instructions, and independently manages her medications and finances. 

Laboratory studies drawn this morning revealed hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, white blood cell count 5.6 ×10⁹/L, platelets 210 ×10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 15 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL (estimated glomerular filtration rate >90 mL/min/1.73 m² with no known chronic kidney disease), AST 22 U/L, ALT 19 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 156 U/L (elevated relative to her baseline, attributed to bony involvement), total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, INR 1.0, fasting glucose 118 mg/dL, and LDL cholesterol 63 mg/dL. Urinalysis was negative for protein, blood, or ketones. An electrocardiogram demonstrated normal sinus rhythm without Q waves, ST-segment deviation, or T-wave inversion. Right-sided ankle–brachial index obtained with Doppler measured 0.64, whereas the left was 0.94. Plain radiographs of the right foot showed no underlying osteomyelitis. 

The patient seeks assessment of the leg symptoms and toe ulcer in the context of her ongoing disseminated breast cancer and otherwise stable cardiometabolic status prior to consideration of supervised exercise therapy versus possible vascular intervention.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) sums age points and weighted comorbidities, counting only the highest applicable category for each condition.
- Age 62 (60–69 years): 2 points.
- Metastatic solid tumor: breast cancer with bone and lung metastases → 6 points. Do not add separate points for the primary tumor.
- Peripheral vascular disease: reproducible exertional calf pain relieved by rest and a right ankle–brachial index of 0.64 establish symptomatic arterial disease → 1 point.
- Diabetes treated with metformin: only mild background retinal changes, without advanced retinopathy, nephropathy, or neuropathy → 1 point.
- Other CCI conditions: none documented → 0 points.
Total = 2 + 6 + 1 + 1 = 10.
Final answer: 10
